item.title: Fire fighters investigating a gas leak turn out to be the cause
item.description:
Fire fighters investigating a gas leak turn out to be the cause

September 23, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

When the residents of the Brabant town of Oisterwijk smelled the pungent odor of gas on Wednesday, they called their local fire department, who turned out to be the culprits.

Fire fighters spent the morning searching for a gas leak to no avail. Together with gas provider Enexis, they tested levels throughout the town but could not find a source, only the smell.

Meanwhile, back at the fire station, staff discovered a canister of THT was missing. The chemical is added to gas, which is naturally odorless, to so that people can smell any leak immediately.

The cannister had been accidently thrown out and had spent the morning in the back of a garbage truck, which was making its rounds.

“We were able to have a laugh about it for a moment,” firefighter Ronald Blokpoel told Omroep Brabant.

Residents may continue to smell gas for a time while the chemical dissipates. The fire depart warns there is no danger to public health.

item.title: Mourners claim diabetic man who died under arrest was “murdered”
item.description:
Mourners claim diabetic man who died under arrest was “murdered”

September 23, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Around 150 people joined a funeral procession on Wednesday for a man who died while being detained by police who stopped him while searching for a stolen fatbike.

The body of 51-year-old Alfredo Goeloe was carried in a white coffin in a carriage drawn by two white horses to the Zuiderbegraafplaats in Rotterdam, 10 days after he collapsed while being pinned to the ground and handcuffed.

Friends and relatives who followed the coffin carried banners with slogans including “samen tegen onrecht omdat we om elkaar geven” (united against injustice because we care for each other).

One of the mourners, Yenci Vargas, told Nieuwsuur: “He was murdered. I’m not talking about racism, but he was murdered by the negligence and stupidity of the police.”

Another, Marsha Mabosa, said: “Last month we were out in a café and he asked me to dance the bachata. He was a very good dancer. And now we have to miss him in a way that is very unjust.”

Stolen fatbike

Goeloe was stopped by police while riding a fatbike through Rotterdam on the evening of Saturday, September 12.

Police initially said he was suspected of stealing the bike, but later changed their story to say he had been stopped because he was riding too fast. Just before Goeloe’s arrest a fatbike had been reported stolen by a couple aged around 40.

Goeloe tried to run from police when they tried to arrest him for not carrying ID. His family said he had borrowed his sister’s bike to go out to get medication for his diabetes.

He was chased down and passed out while he was being restrained on his belly. Video footage showed he cried out that he had diabetes and was in pain as he lay on the ground.

Official complaint

Goeloe’s family have filed a criminal complaint against four police officers. Lawyer Gerard Roethof said they viewed it as “a case of manslaughter, or in any event severe assault with fatal consequences.”

Jan Schalkwijk, a lawyer with Control Alt Delete, an organisation that monitors racial profiling in the Netherlands, said the use of force by police was excessive.

“The officers were far superior in number, according to reports he was unarmed, and he could have been approached with less force,” Schalkwijk argued.

Restraint guidelines

But Jaap Timmer, a political scientist at the VU university in Amsterdam who specialises in police use of force, said there was no indication from the film footage that the police had failed to follow protocol.

He said police guidelines said people should be pressed against the ground for as short a time as possible when under arrest, but it was unsafe to let them stand up before they had been handcuffed.

“I understand the police were looking for a fatbike and this man was riding too fast. That could be a reason to ask his identity,” he said.

“He then ran away fast and resisted his arrest. That has nothing to do with ethnic profiling, but with the man’s behaviour.”

item.title: Road safety institute weighing up zero alcohol limit for drivers
item.description:
Road safety institute weighing up zero alcohol limit for drivers

September 23, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

The Dutch Road Safety Research Institute has released a new study on reducing the drug and alcohol limit for drivers to zero, finding it would probably decrease road accidents but would increase pressure on the police.

SWOV looked at the policy in eight countries with limits lower than the Netherlands, which is of blood alcohol level of 0.05% or 0.02% for those who have been driving for less than 5 years.

The risk of accidents is already elevated at the 0.05% level, the report says. Other countries, including Norway and Sweden, set the level at 0.02% for all drivers.

“An absolute zero limit is considered to be a simple and unambiguous standard that leaves less room for interpretation of what is still permissible and what is not,” the report says, and would improve road safety.

However, lowering the limit will lead to more work for police but also testing facilities. It can be difficult, especially with cannabis, to properly detect the levels, especially with saliva tests.

“Particularly for THC and cocaine, concentrations or metabolites can remain detectable long after the immediate effects have disappeared,” the institute wrote, which would create legal problems for criminal prosecutions.

item.title: Water used to put out waste plant fire contaminated with PFAS
item.description:
Water used to put out waste plant fire contaminated with PFAS

September 23, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Firefighters used water contaminated with PFAS chemicals to put out a blaze at a waste processing plant in Gelderland that was operating illegally.

Aalden municipal council said the water would have to be pumped out of the sewage network to prevent it polluting drinking water supplies, because the purification system is not able to filter it out.

The blaze in Dinxperlo, a village on the German border, burned for several hours on Monday night after a large pile of wood chippings caught fire, covering an area of 20m by 30m at its height.

Firefighters pumped water from Het Blauwe Meer, a nearby recreational lake that has been closed to swimmers since 2024 because of high levels of PFAS. Most of the water subsequently drained away into the sewage system.

The council said it was investigating the impact, but there was no reason to avoid drinking tap water. “At the moment there are no consequences for the use of the sewage network by residents,” a spokesman said.

Police are also investigating the fire. The waste processing plant was shut down in November 2025 on the orders of the council for “serious breaches of environmental regulations.”

No permits

The operators burned large quantities of waste that they did not have permits for and mixed different types of waste that should have been separated, the council found.

Recent studies found that high levels of PFAS are present in Dutch drinking water supplies, particularly in western areas where the water is taken from rivers that have been contaminated by agricultural use.

PFAS chemicals are widely used in pesticides, packaging and products ranging from waterproof clothing to non-stick cooking pans.

They are known as “forever chemicals” because of their high durability, but have also been linked to illnesses such as cancer, diseases of the immune system and complications in unborn babies.

The public health agency RIVM has called for a total ban on PFAS in pesticides by the EU, a move also supported in Germany and the Scandinavian nations.

item.title: The IamExpat Fair is back in Eindhoven: what’s new this year?
item.description:
Partner content

The IamExpat Fair is back in Eindhoven: what’s new this year?

September 23, 2026

The IamExpat Fair returns to Eindhoven on Saturday October 3 for its second outing in the city, with a bigger careers section, two international centres and a new kids area.

The fair, which takes place in the Klokgebouw in Strijp-S, provides advice and services of all kinds for the international community, including special offers only available for attendees. You can register for free online.

“We are bringing back the large career section, expanding the number of expat centres at the fair, and growing the Family & Kids section,” says event manager Claire Leunissen.

Workshops and presentations 
The fair will also feature over 20 free workshops to help expats with job hunting, finding housing, immigration and settling advice, as well as tips on local leisure and health services, and more. The workshops have limited capacity and are filling up fast, so make sure to book seats as soon as possible — you can sign up here.

Careers and partners
The careers section includes Brainport and recruitment agency Undutchables, and offers additional advice and services for the partners of people who have moved to the region for work.

“The international community of Eindhoven can’t be underestimated,” says Claire. “Because of this small but mighty community, we are bringing the Fair back to Eindhoven to support internationals and their families looking to to settle into Dutch life as well, through career opportunities, community groups, fitness schools, Dutch classes, and more.”

Families and newcomers
New this year is a kids area, supervised by childcare provider Korein, where families can play while parents work their way round the stands.

Two international centres will be on hand for questions about registration and residency: Holland Expat Center South, based in Eindhoven, and Expat Centre Maastricht Region. Orion Immigration Law returns with a stand double the size of last year’s.

Language schools include Language Institute Regina Coeli in Vught, Una Paloma Blanca, Bart de Pau and Taalkracht, while the health and leisure exhibitors range from bike subscription service Swapfiets to Happy Bodies and Shakti Nutrition.

Every stage covered
Workshops and presentations by experts run for most of the day, covering renting, buying a house and securing a mortgage, tax, careers and schooling.

“The fair is an incredible one-stop shop for every part of life in the Netherlands,” says Claire. “International students or young professionals may initially come to the Fair looking for Dutch language classes or career opportunities, but later in life, they come to the Fair for different needs, such as preparing for retirement, buying their first home, or choosing the right daycare for their kids.”

“We are excited to bring the IamExpat Fair back to the Klokgebouw, a historic building that embodies the history of technology, innovation and immigration of Eindhoven,” says Claire.

The IamExpat Fair Eindhoven takes place in the Klokgebouw, Strijp-S on Saturday October 3 from 10am to 5pm. Entrance is free with online registration.

item.title: Support for refugees should prioritise finding skilled work: SER
item.description:
Support for refugees should prioritise finding skilled work: SER

September 23, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

The government needs to do more to help settled asylum seekers find work that matches their skills as part of their integration into society, a new report by the socio-economic council (SER) advises.

Municipalities should have a legal obligation to support newcomers find suitable work, with financial input from The Hague, rather than leaving asylum seekers to search for jobs on their own.

The report said the current requirements were unclear and had contradictory aims, with the obligation on new migrants to learn the language and learn citizenship making it harder for them to work.

“At the moment people often have language lessons, with travel time as well. In practice that is often hard to combine with working,” a spokesman told NOS. “We say people should able to work or train and the question is how to organise language and citizenship around that.”

The cabinet has said it wants asylum seekers to be able to start looking for work after three months, rather than the current waiting period of six, but the plan still has to go through parliament.

Currently only 57% of refugees with settled status are working eight years after they are given permission to stay, compared to 81% of the entire working-age population.

Not just numbers

Work and participation minister Thierry Aartsen has set a target of getting 75,000 newcomers into work, but the SER said the numbers should not be the only issue.

The report said there was a risk of skilled migrants being locked in to jobs that did not reflect their talents. “Settled refugees and displaced Ukrainians are often employed in basic agency work that doesn’t reflect their education, experience and ambitions. For them, basic work is not a stepping-stone to a better job.”

A report by the national auditor this year concluded that the Netherlands was missing opportunities to address skills shortages by employing settled refugees in sectors with vacancies.

The SER also said financial support for language lessons should be restored for Ukrainian refugees so they had the same right as other asylum seekers. Settled refugees receive financial support up to B2 level, but this has been stopped for Ukrainians.

Yana Shcherbak, who worked as a doctor in Ukraine for 15 years before the Russian invasion, said she was held back when she first arrived in Amsterdam by the confusing and disjointed rules. “I didn’t know there were language lessons for a year,” she said.

She now works as a dental and psychiatric assistant, but hopes to retrain at Amsterdam’s OVLG hospital. “I often dream that I’m working in the hospital again, in a white coat,” she told the SER. “Then I wake up and realise where I am.”

item.title: The pen is mightier than the scrub: hospitals warn of ink stains
item.description:
The pen is mightier than the scrub: hospitals warn of ink stains

September 23, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Utrecht University Medical Centre is warning its doctors and nurses to check their pockets before putting their scrubs in the wash, as ink stains have become a spot of problem for the laundry.

According to RTL, hundreds of uniforms are thrown away in Dutch hospitals because markets and ballpoint pens end up in the washing machine.

A spokesperson for laundry company CleanLease, which manages the laundry for the Utrecht hospital, says scrubs and other laundry items are sent through an X-ray before getting wet. “We detect 99 percent of the items. But pens and markers are a persistent problem,” they told RTL.

A single pen can cause an entire load of uniforms to be rejected. For UMC Utrecht, this amounts to 50 uniforms per week.

“In healthcare, we already have a shortage of materials, staff, and costs. That is why we must return to common sense and look at the simplest solution: just check your jacket and trouser pockets and take that pen out,” Celina Kroon, sustainability manager at UMC Utrecht, said.

item.title: Dutch economy grew by 0.6% in Q2, faster than initially thought
item.description:
Dutch economy grew by 0.6% in Q2, faster than initially thought

September 23, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

The Dutch economy grew by 0.6% in the second quarter of 2026, more than the national statistic agency CBS’s initial assessment.

The CBS said higher export volumes and stronger household spending were the main reasons for the revision. The second, more detailed assessment is published around 85 days after the end of the quarter.

Over the 12-month period GDP grew by 1.6%, its fastest rate since the first quarter of 2025. That figure was also revised upwards from an initial 1.3%.

The labour market improved, with an additional 15,000 employees and registered freelancers in the second quarter. The initial assessment said the total number of jobs had dropped by 8,000.

item.title: Netherlands sets out route map to phase out fossil fuels
item.description:
Netherlands sets out route map to phase out fossil fuels

September 22, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

The Netherlands has become the second country in the world to publish detailed plans of how it intends to end its dependence on fossil fuels.

The Dutch government followed France in outlining a so-called “route map” to phasing out oil, gas and coal, in the run-up to the UN Climate Change Conference in Turkey in November.

The plan drew praise from international climate change experts for giving definition to the Netherlands’ ambitions, but there was also criticism for the failure to set a firm deadline.

The decision to draw up national route maps was an outcome of a smaller-scale summit organised by the Netherlands and Colombia in April to discuss moving away from fossil fuels, which 50 countries attended.

France was the first country to publish its plan, which was mostly a summary of existing policies and targets, such as ending the use of coal by 2030, oil by 2045 and gas by 2050.

The Dutch plan includes a reassertion of its commitment to stop using coal-fired power stations to produce electricity by 2030, but other targets have been delayed or downgraded.

Goals downgraded

The Netherlands has reduced the amount of wind energy it wants to produce at sea, abandoned its goal of making the electricity network CO2 free by 2035 and will not meet the EU’s target of reducing emissions by 90% by 2040.

Natalie Jones, of the International Institute for Sustainable Development, said the Dutch plan was a “good example for other countries”.

But climate campaigners were more critical. Maarten de Zeeuw of Greenpeace Nederland told Trouw: “The biggest problem is that unlike France, there is no clear end date. You can call it a route map, but you don’t know where the route is going.”

Joyeeta Gupta, professor of environment and development at the University of Amsterdam, said the plan did not go far enough, given that the limit for global warming of 1.5 degrees C, set in the 2015 Paris Agreement, has almost been reached.

“Already 25 million people a year are fleeing because of the climate crisis, and that is just one of the many terrible consequences,” she said.

A spokesman for the Dutch environment ministry said the route map reflected the Netherlands’ ambition to lead the group of countries that wanted to take a pro-active role on climate change. “The fact that we have made our own route map helps our credibility,” the spokesman said.

item.title: Prosecutors demand jail for blast that killed three in drugs lab
item.description:
Prosecutors demand jail for blast that killed three in drugs lab

September 22, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Prosecutors have demanded a seven-year jail sentence for a man who blew up a drugs lab in Rotterdam, causing a blast that killed three people and damaged neighbouring flats.

Jalal O., 37, was renting the garage store on Schammenkamp to produce cocaine when it exploded on the evening of January 29, 2024. One of the victims was his 22-year-old cousin, who was working in the lab at the time.

A forensic investigation found that the blast was caused by vats of acetone, used in the production of the drug, catching fire at the back of the building. A neighbouring block of flats was so badly damaged that five homes had to be demolished.

Prosecutors said O. had “allowed financial gain to prevail over the safety of local residents and others”. They said he had sublet the property via a “shady arrangement”.

O. helped with the search for missing neighbours immediately after the disaster, but was arrested a few days later. He told the district court in Rotterdam he found the events “terrible”, but denied that he was using the garage for drug production.

Prosecutors produces messages between O. and his cousin showing steam rising from barrels of acetone, while residents complained of the chemical smells from the building. The prosecution said the defendant’s denials were “totally unbelievable”.

One woman who was evacuated from one of the flats said the explosion had had a devastating effect on her health.

“I have lost part of my hearing, my hair has fallen out and I have lost my teeth through stress,” she said. “I have flashbacks and sleep badly. I have nightmares in which I fall into the fire and burn to death.”
